extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, sociologists, criminologists, and communication researchers studying race/ethnicity in television crime news
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing TV crime news race portrayals
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analytic and multivariate modeling of how situational story features and Designated Market Area (DMA) contextual characteristics predict the reported race/ethnicity of perpetrators and victims in television crime news (local and national).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power structure argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The race or ethnicity of those with power in the media (ownership, reporters, anchors) affects story selection and how groups are represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that because most media owners and key decision-makers are White, minorities will be overrepresented as offenders and underrepresented as victims; biases and world-views of those who select and shape stories may be reflected in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market share perspective / newsworthiness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition for market share drives media to focus on stories that draw viewers, advance careers, or draw on important sources (e.g., law enforcement). Newsworthiness criteria include timeliness, proximity, novelty, prominence, conflict, magnitude, and human interest (Shoemaker & Reese 1996).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coverage follows market share logic, situational factors that increase newsworthiness will be used to cater to largest audiences; this can lead to increased representation of Whites (as both perpetrators and victims) if that attracts viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal crimes (Sudnow) / deviance types
rubrics_metrics.description: Many crimes are 'normal' with typical social characteristics; unusual or deviant crimes attract greater attention. Three forms of deviance: statistical deviance, status deviance, and cultural deviance (Pritchard & Hughes 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical deviance (rarity) and status deviance (departure from high-status, white-male norm) predict more coverage of White perpetrators/victims; cultural deviance depends on acts (drugs/gangs/especially vulnerable victims) and is not inherently about race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial threat perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant groups perceive large minority populations as threatening political/economic prerogatives; this can influence social control and representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In DMAs with higher percentages of Blacks/Hispanics or higher violent crime rates, expect greater representation of Blacks and Hispanics as perpetrators and possibly less as victims; applies at contextual (DMA) level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial privilege / victim devaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The justice system and media may take crimes against White victims more seriously; victimization of persons of color is devalued while White victims are privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater media representation of White victims than minority victims; privileging may be especially pronounced for White female victims given historical legacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational story-level predictors (story characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story-level situational features affecting representation: violent index offense (murder, robbery, forcible rape, aggravated assault), number of victims (multiple victims), victim gender (female), novelty/unusual circumstances, prominence, conflict, magnitude, human interest, proximity, timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features increase newsworthiness and are expected (depending on theoretical perspective) to influence whether Whites or minorities appear as reported perpetrators or victims — e.g., violent index crimes, multiple victims, and female victims are predicted (by power structure/racial privilege) to be associated with reporting minority perpetrators and White victims; market share predicts increased reporting of Whites in both roles when newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social structural / DMA contextual predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual DMA-level measures used to predict representation include percent Black, percent Hispanic, violent index crime rate, population size, and region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contextual characteristics are included in multivariate models; racial threat expects more minority-as-offender reporting where minority percentages and violent crime rates are higher; market share suggests both minority perpetrators and victims may increase with larger minority populations; racial privilege predicts more White victims in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline models / competing hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary expectations derived from theoretical perspectives: power structure/racial threat/privilege predict Blacks and Hispanics overrepresented as offenders and underrepresented as victims, Whites underrepresented as offenders and overrepresented as victims; market share/normal crimes suggest Whites overrepresented as both perpetrators and victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use baseline models to compare empirical patterns and adjudicate between theoretical expectations; recognize contradictory expectations across perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of comparison for 'accuracy' of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Three comparison standards for evaluating representation: intergroup (one group vs another), interrole (portrayal as perpetrator vs victim), interreality (media representation vs crime statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should report and interpret representation patterns relative to these standards separately, as conclusions depend on which standard is used (e.g., a group can be overrepresented by one standard and not by another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis and story inclusion/exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit: television news stories that make explicit mention of current, specific violent crimes. Excluded: stories about violent crime in general without a specific incident, policy/program stories, civil cases (unless they involve a violent crime), terrorism, sports violence among participants, government-sponsored violence, historical violent crimes, uncontrolled animal attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these inclusion/exclusion rules to ensure comparable, incident-specific content; coder training should emphasize these boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling design and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratified random sample of television newscasts (2002–2003) using 'constructed months' (stratified by quarter and day of week) and DMAs stratified into six strata by market size; one evening news broadcast per DMA stratum per date; national networks (ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC) sampled separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design seeks national representativeness of local news coverage across market sizes; control for national vs local broadcasts in analysis; use county-to-DMA aggregation to build contextual measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content coding procedures and reliability checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories were content coded by two trained graduate students with regular meetings to refine the coding scheme; identification of violent crime stories was double-coded at multiple points; Cohen's kappas for identification ranged from .76 to over .9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double-coding, iterative coder meetings, and periodic reliability checks (e.g., at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% milestones) to ensure coding quality; report kappas for key variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of race/ethnicity and handling small categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported race/ethnicity of perpetrators and victims is coded (White, Black, Hispanic emphasized). Integrated groups and very small categories were folded into existing categories (treated as minority) to avoid excluding cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about category decisions and rationale (e.g., low cell counts); note potential biases introduced by folding groups into broader categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variables: reported race/ethnicity of perpetrators and victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat perpetrators' and victims' reported race/ethnicity as outcomes (modeled separately) to examine predictors of whether the story reports a subject as White, Black, or Hispanic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model perpetrators and victims separately because predictors and patterns may differ by role; report models that control for situational and contextual variables simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external data sources for contextual validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual measures are constructed from external sources: Census 2000 for DMA population composition and FBI Uniform Crime Reports (UCR) for criminal offending rates (2002–2003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map counties to DMAs using authoritative sources (Broadcasting and Cable Yearbook, Nielsen) and aggregate counts appropriately; use external statistics for interreality comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling of national networks and local stations with control
rubrics_metrics.description: National network stories (ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC) are sampled separately from local DMA broadcasts; analyses control for whether a story is from national versus local broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include broadcast type as a covariate to isolate differences driven by national vs local news practices and sampling frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling low-frequency situational variables (measurement limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some potentially important situational features (e.g., alcohol and drug use) occur in <4% of stories and thus cannot be reliably estimated and were excluded from models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report when variables are omitted for low prevalence; interpret model results with caution for omitted situational elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls: population size and region
rubrics_metrics.description: Population size of DMA and U.S. region are included as control variables in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these controls to account for macro-level differences in market characteristics and regional variation in coverage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized situational-context interaction expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that situational features (violent index offenses, multiple victims, female victims) interact with power structure/privilege to yield reporting patterns (e.g., minority perpetrators and White victims in more newsworthy contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test conditional hypotheses and interaction effects in multivariate models; examine whether situational factors amplify or attenuate contextual effects.
